title: TamedFlow: Trajectory-Aware Distillationfor Teacher-Assisted Diffusion Sampling

paper.title: TamedFlow: Trajectory-Aware Distillation for Teacher-Assisted Diffusion Sampling
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) deliver high-fidelity image and video generation, but inference requires many sequential model evaluations. Two acceleration strategies are increasingly important: model compression makes each evaluation cheaper, while adaptive inference avoids selected teacher computation through reuse, forecasting, or speculative execution. Their combination, however, is brittle: directly applying the evaluated adaptive methods to a compressed student can degrade quality, an observed failure mode we call the Combination Gap . We link this gap to a mismatch between pointwise distillation and short-horizon execution: a student trained at teacher states need not remain reliable when its own predictions are chained. We propose TamedFlow , which trains a compressed DiT for this deployed role through cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision. At inference, a lightweight Learnable Trajectory Estimator routes completed drafts: accepted drafts bypass the teacher, while rejected drafts roll back and receive one teacher rescue step. Distilling DiT-XL/2 into DiT-B/2, TamedFlow reaches FID 2.58 2.58 at 2.25 × 2.25\times measured speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Ablations support trajectory supervision, and routing controls favor LTE over random decisions at nearly matched latency. Evaluations on ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 , MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics extend the empirical scope.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become a leading backbone for high-fidelity visual generation ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , yet iterative denoising imposes high inference latency. Each sample requires dozens of sequential forward passes, with costs scaling rapidly with model parameters, resolution, and sequence length. Existing acceleration strategies attack complementary aspects of this cost: step-reduction methods shorten the solver schedule ( Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) ; parameter compression lowers per-step computation; and adaptive inference reuses or forecasts intermediate activations ( Ma et al., 2024b ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . Combining parameter compression with adaptive execution is intuitively appealing, promising cheaper evaluations while skipping redundant computation. All headline experiments below use fixed-step DDIM integration to evaluate compression and adaptive execution under a unified solver convention. In practice, this composition can break down. In our controlled diagnostic (Appendix Table 11 ), attaching the evaluated adaptive reuse methods directly to a compressed student degrades sample quality, inflating ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 FID from 5.56 5.56 to between 10.40 10.40 and 13.18 13.18 . We term this failure mode the Combination Gap . This result exposes an operational mismatch: a student trained for pointwise agreement need not remain reliable after its own predictions alter the states encountered later. Rather than applying internal reuse unchanged to the compact model, we let the student generate short trajectory drafts and reserve teacher intervention for drafts predicted to deviate. Figure 1: The Combination Gap and TamedFlow. Directly applying adaptive reuse to a parameter-compressed student severely degrades quality in our diagnostic. TamedFlow instead trains the compressed student for short-horizon trajectory agreement. A 4M-parameter LTE routes drafts: accepted drafts bypass the teacher; rejected drafts roll back for one teacher rescue step. Chaining student predictions into drafts, however, introduces compounding integration drift. Proposition 3.1 characterizes this through an Euler rollout bound: spatial sensitivity can amplify local student–teacher velocity mismatch over sequential steps. To stabilize drafting against this amplification, we introduce TamedFlow , combining trajectory-aware distillation with selective teacher rescue (Figure 1 ). During training, cross-architecture feature alignment (AlignNet) grounds student representations in teacher layers; a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head (VAH) absorbs residual velocity errors; and randomized K K -step rollout supervision ( K ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 1 , 5 ) K\sim\mathcal{U}(1,5) ) penalizes both intermediate mismatch and accumulated endpoint drift. A two-stage curriculum introduces the multi-step objectives only after feature alignment. At inference, TamedFlow uses an asymmetric execution policy. A compact Learnable Trajectory Estimator (LTE, 4M parameters) scores completed drafts from pooled student tokens and timestep embeddings without teacher access. If confidence exceeds threshold τ \tau , the draft is accepted, advancing K K steps while bypassing the teacher. If rejected, the sampler rolls back to the pre-draft state and advances one step with teacher rescue. Varying τ \tau selects among measured operating points between throughput and fidelity without sequential teacher verification. Distilling DiT-XL/2 into a 130M DiT-B/2 student on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , TamedFlow attains FID 2.58 2.58 at 2.25 × 2.25\times measured speedup ( 0.464 0.464 s vs. 1.044 1.044 s) over the DDIM-50 teacher. At comparable latency, TamedFlow improves FID over the evaluated training-free adaptive baselines (e.g., FoCa at FID 2.65 2.65 , 0.466 0.466 s). Controlled ablations support trajectory supervision and learned routing at nearly matched latency, while evaluations on ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 , MS-COCO, and Latte video DiTs extend the empirical scope. In summary, our contributions are: • Diagnostic and analysis of the Combination Gap. We document the failure of applying the evaluated adaptive reuse methods to a compressed DiT, and derive a DDIM rollout bound characterizing how sequential drafting can amplify local velocity errors. • Trajectory-stabilized speculative distillation. We introduce TamedFlow, uniting feature alignment, residual velocity correction, and randomized rollout supervision to optimize a compressed DiT for autonomous multi-step drafting. • Learned routing and deployment evaluation. We propose an asymmetric execution policy via a 4M-parameter LTE to accept reliable drafts or trigger teacher rescue, evaluating quality–latency trade-offs across resolutions, text conditioning, and video alongside physical deployment costs.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Prior work on DiT acceleration reduces the number of solver evaluations, the cost of each evaluation, or the teacher computation retained during adaptive execution. TamedFlow studies their interface: whether a compressed student can reliably replace short segments of a teacher trajectory.

sections.heading: 2.1 Step Count Reduction in Diffusion and Flow Models
sections.text: Step reduction lowers the number of solver evaluations. Higher-order solvers improve numerical efficiency for a fixed model ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , while distillation changes the model: progressive distillation shortens the schedule ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , consistency models match predictions across noise levels ( Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) , MeanFlow and Model-Guidance alter the target or absorb guidance ( Geng et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . Other formulations align distributions or scores, distill autoregressively, transfer trajectories, or train few-step students adversarially ( Yin et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) . These methods optimize a sparse standalone sampler deployed entirely on its own. TamedFlow instead retains a multi-step teacher as a reliable safeguard and uses the student to propose short trajectory segments whose acceptance is decided adaptively online. A related line studies trajectory geometry. Rectified flow and InstaFlow construct straighter paths ( Liu et al., 2023 ) ; interpolant transformers unify diffusion and flow parametrizations ( Ma et al., 2024a ) ; and guided path sampling corrects trajectories during integration ( Li et al., 2026 ) . TCD and Hyper-SD learn consistency or trajectory segments for few-step sampling ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2024 ) . TamedFlow keeps the teacher path as the reference, trains a cross-architecture student for selectively accepted rollouts, and retains teacher rescue in the deployed sampler.

sections.heading: 2.2 Per-Step Compute Acceleration and Feature Caching
sections.text: Per-step methods keep the schedule while avoiding full recomputation. Feature-reuse methods cache activations across timesteps or blocks ( Ma et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2026b ; Wimbauer et al., 2024 ) ; forecasting methods extrapolate future features ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Cai et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) ; and learned schedulers select policies per sample ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . These methods exploit local regularity in intermediate computations. Our same-student diagnostic shows that their evaluated configurations do not transfer directly to the compressed student, but does not isolate a universal caching failure mechanism. Most reuse methods leave the model unchanged and decide which internal computations can be skipped. TamedFlow instead trains the student under rollout supervision and learns whether an entire student-generated segment can advance without a teacher call. DisCa ( Zou et al., 2026a ) also studies incompatibility between step-distilled video DiTs and feature caches, but repairs the cache side with a predictor and Restricted MeanFlow schedule. TamedFlow acts on the draft student instead.

sections.heading: 2.3 Speculative Verification in Generative Paradigms
sections.text: Speculative decoding verifies proposed tokens with a target model ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ) ; causal masking permits parallel verification and exact correction. Diffusion lacks this structure because each teacher state depends on the preceding prediction. Replaying a K K -step draft exactly would require sequential teacher evaluations and remove much of the saving. SpecDiff ( Pan et al., 2026 ) studies self-speculative diffusion under this constraint. TamedFlow replaces exact verification with learned trajectory estimation. The LTE scores student-internal features after a draft using rollout agreement as its training target. Accepted drafts avoid the teacher; rejected drafts return to the pre-draft state for one teacher step. Routing is therefore inexpensive and online, but approximate and not distribution-preserving by construction.

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries: Diffusion Models, DiT, and Flow Matching
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) learn to reverse a gradual noising process, so generation requires a sequence of state-dependent model evaluations. A Diffusion Transformer (DiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) implements the denoiser with a transformer over latent patches and injects timestep and condition information through adaptive layer normalization. Our method is expressed in velocity form because both its trajectory loss and its stability analysis act on the vector field followed during sampling. Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) casts generation as a probability-path ODE. sections.heading: Models and datasets.
sections.text: The primary setting distills a 675M DiT-XL/2 teacher 𝒯 ϕ \mathcal{T}_{\phi} ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) into a 130M DiT-B/2 student ℬ θ \mathcal{B}_{\theta} on class-conditional ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 . We evaluate resolution scaling on ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 , text conditioning on MS-COCO, and video generation with Latte on FaceForensics. For COCO, a shared 19.9M text-conditioning adapter maps 77-token CLIP ViT-L/14 features into the DiT conditioning space; the teacher and student use this shared adapter while the ImageNet-trained VAH and LTE remain fixed. For Latte, the student, AlignNet, VAH, and LTE are retrained for the evaluated video-DiT setting. Complete training schedules, solver settings, and adaptation protocols are provided in Appendices A and E .

sections.heading: Metrics and reporting.
sections.text: On ImageNet, we report FID-50K and Inception Score (IS); on MS-COCO, FID-30K and CLIP-Score computed with OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14; and on FaceForensics, FVD and video Inception Score. Image and text-to-image wall-clock latency and speedup are measured on a single A800-80GB GPU at batch size one and averaged over 10 runs. All baseline rows are measured in our local implementations under the same reporting protocol. Speedup is normalized to the corresponding teacher, and the LTE accept rate is the fraction of routing events that retain the student draft. FLOPs count backbone evaluations, whereas latency also includes VAH, LTE, rollback, and solver overhead.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against schedule-reduction references (DDIM-25 and DDIM-20), full-scale few-step distillation methods (Progressive Distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , LCM ( Luo et al., 2023 ) , and ARD ( Kim et al., 2025 ) ), and adaptive or speculative methods ( Δ \Delta -DiT ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , FoCa ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , FORA ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) , SpeCa ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , and SpecDiff ( Pan et al., 2026 ) ). Adaptive and speculative baselines are re-implemented in the matched DiT-XL/2 pipeline and measured locally under the same latency protocol. Few-step distillation baselines use the full teacher architecture without parameter compression. Appendix B details the comparison scope and accounting assumptions.

sections.heading: Quality–latency operating points.
sections.text: Table 1 compares complete systems across speedup regimes. Four-step distillation baselines attain aggressive 14 × 14\times – 15 × 15\times acceleration at the cost of severe FID degradation. TamedFlow instead targets moderate acceleration with tight quality retention: at τ = 0.85 \tau=0.85 , it matches the DDIM-50 teacher within 0.02 0.02 FID ( 2.33 2.33 vs. 2.35 2.35 ) at 1.73 × 1.73\times speedup; at default τ = 0.80 \tau=0.80 , it reaches FID 2.58 2.58 at 2.25 × 2.25\times speedup ( 0.464 0.464 s). In the 2.0 × 2.0\times to 2.5 × 2.5\times range under nearly matched latencies around 0.46 0.46 to 0.48 0.48 seconds, TamedFlow achieves better quality than FoCa at FID 2.65 2.65 and TaylorSeer at FID 2.73 2.73 , alongside a higher Inception Score. This represents a quality advantage at matched latency rather than a throughput claim from millisecond-scale differences. Although SpeCa reports lower backbone FLOPs of 4.76 4.76 T, its FID is 0.20 0.20 worse, and backbone FLOPs omit runtime overheads like rollback, VAH, and LTE that are fully captured by measured latency. Thus, TamedFlow’s edge lies in its empirical Pareto trade-off for the deployed system, not a FLOPs-only claim.

sections.heading: Qualitative study.
sections.text: Figure 3 compares generated samples under matched speedup ( 2.1 × 2.1\times – 2.25 × 2.25\times ). TamedFlow preserves fine textures and object boundaries more cleanly across diverse classes. For example, it avoids the over-smoothed fur patterns on Tabby and Boxer seen in competing adaptive methods, and retains clear structural separation between the metal hoops and wood grain on Barrel . These visual examples align with aggregate FID trends, while the following ablations isolate the underlying mechanisms. Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 .

sections.heading: Deployment cost.
sections.text: TamedFlow requires offline training and maintains the teacher, student, VAH, and LTE co-resident in memory, increasing peak allocated VRAM from 2.570 2.570 to 3.075 3.075 GB ( ∼ \sim 0.5 GB overhead). This footprint reflects the deliberate choice to retain a high-capacity teacher for selective rescue rather than discarding it. Headline latency is benchmarked for batch-one latent integration without VAE decoding, characterizing interactive generation rather than batched serving throughput. Teacher offloading and weight quantization represent orthogonal opportunities to mitigate co-residency overhead in production.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced TamedFlow, an acceleration framework that reconciles parameter compression with adaptive execution for Diffusion Transformers. By training a compact student for short-horizon trajectory agreement and employing asymmetric routing with selective teacher rescue, TamedFlow achieves FID 2.58 2.58 at 2.25 × 2.25\times speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , with transfer evaluated across resolutions, text conditioning, and video. Our findings show that pointwise alignment can leave compounding trajectory divergence during autonomous drafting, creating the Combination Gap. Controlled ablations support rollout supervision, and routing controls favor LTE over random decisions at nearly matched latency, suggesting that compression and adaptive inference can be made compatible when the compact model is trained as a multi-step drafter and the sampler retains a recovery path back to the teacher.

sections.heading: Appendix K Limitations
sections.text: While TamedFlow provides empirical gains across several settings, our findings are subject to several key limitations:

sections.heading: Theoretical scope of rollout analysis.
sections.text: The discrete Grönwall bound in Proposition 3.1 characterizes error accumulation under sequential Euler drafting to motivate multi-step trajectory supervision. It does not constitute a universal failure law for internal feature caching or forecasting methods, nor does it provide formal convergence or stability guarantees for higher-order ODE solvers such as DPM-Solver++.

sections.heading: Approximate nature of trajectory routing.
sections.text: The Learnable Trajectory Estimator (LTE) operates as an empirical regression model trained on offline consistency targets rather than an exact, distribution-preserving verification mechanism. Rejection decisions are heuristic; false rejections incur latency penalties through redundant teacher evaluations, whereas false acceptances may allow minor perceptual artifacts to propagate into the generated sample.

sections.heading: Deployment and infrastructure overhead.
sections.text: TamedFlow relies on a multi-stage offline training curriculum and maintains the teacher, student, VAH, and LTE models co-resident in GPU memory during inference ( ∼ 0.5 \sim 0.5 GB VRAM overhead in our FP32 profile). As a result, it does not fully eliminate the teacher model from deployment. Furthermore, our reported speedups reflect batch-size-one latent generation on single GPUs; characterization under large-batch throughput, concurrent serving pipelines, and extreme memory-constrained edge environments remains an avenue for future work.

Xuming Hu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Abstract Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) deliver high-fidelity image and video generation, but inference requires many sequential model evaluations. Two acceleration strategies are increasingly important: model compression makes each evaluation cheaper, while adaptive inference avoids selected teacher computation through reuse, forecasting, or speculative execution. Their combination, however, is brittle: directly applying the evaluated adaptive methods to a compressed student can degrade quality, an observed failure mode we call the Combination Gap . We link this gap to a mismatch between pointwise distillation and short-horizon execution: a student trained at teacher states need not remain reliable when its own predictions are chained. We propose TamedFlow , which trains a compressed DiT for this deployed role through cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision. At inference, a lightweight Learnable Trajectory Estimator routes completed drafts: accepted drafts bypass the teacher, while rejected drafts roll back and receive one teacher rescue step. Distilling DiT-XL/2 into DiT-B/2, TamedFlow reaches FID 2.58 2.58 at 2.25 × 2.25\times measured speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Ablations support trajectory supervision, and routing controls favor LTE over random decisions at nearly matched latency. Evaluations on ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 , MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics extend the empirical scope. 1 Introduction Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become a leading backbone for high-fidelity visual generation ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , yet iterative denoising imposes high inference latency. Each sample requires dozens of sequential forward passes, with costs scaling rapidly with model parameters, resolution, and sequence length. Existing acceleration strategies attack complementary aspects of this cost: step-reduction methods shorten the solver schedule ( Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) ; parameter compression lowers per-step computation; and adaptive inference reuses or forecasts intermediate activations ( Ma et al., 2024b ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . Combining parameter compression with adaptive execution is intuitively appealing, promising cheaper evaluations while skipping redundant computation. All headline experiments below use fixed-step DDIM integration to evaluate compression and adaptive execution under a unified solver convention. In practice, this composition can break down. In our controlled diagnostic (Appendix Table 11 ), attaching the evaluated adaptive reuse methods directly to a compressed student degrades sample quality, inflating ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 FID from 5.56 5.56 to between 10.40 10.40 and 13.18 13.18 . We term this failure mode the Combination Gap . This result exposes an operational mismatch: a student trained for pointwise agreement need not remain reliable after its own predictions alter the states encountered later. Rather than applying internal reuse unchanged to the compact model, we let the student generate short trajectory drafts and reserve teacher intervention for drafts predicted to deviate. Figure 1: The Combination Gap and TamedFlow. Directly applying adaptive reuse to a parameter-compressed student severely degrades quality in our diagnostic. TamedFlow instead trains the compressed student for short-horizon trajectory agreement. A 4M-parameter LTE routes drafts: accepted drafts bypass the teacher; rejected drafts roll back for one teacher rescue step. Chaining student predictions into drafts, however, introduces compounding integration drift. Proposition 3.1 characterizes this through an Euler rollout bound: spatial sensitivity can amplify local student–teacher velocity mismatch over sequential steps. To stabilize drafting against this amplification, we introduce TamedFlow , combining trajectory-aware distillation with selective teacher rescue (Figure 1 ). During training, cross-architecture feature alignment (AlignNet) grounds student representations in teacher layers; a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head (VAH) absorbs residual velocity errors; and randomized K K -step rollout supervision ( K ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 1 , 5 ) K\sim\mathcal{U}(1,5) ) penalizes both intermediate mismatch and accumulated endpoint drift. A two-stage curriculum introduces the multi-step objectives only after feature alignment. At inference, TamedFlow uses an asymmetric execution policy. A compact Learnable Trajectory Estimator (LTE, 4M parameters) scores completed drafts from pooled student tokens and timestep embeddings without teacher access. If confidence exceeds threshold τ \tau , the draft is accepted, advancing K K steps while bypassing the teacher. If rejected, the sampler rolls back to the pre-draft state and advances one step with teacher rescue. Varying τ \tau selects among measured operating points between throughput and fidelity without sequential teacher verification. Distilling DiT-XL/2 into a 130M DiT-B/2 student on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , TamedFlow attains FID 2.58 2.58 at 2.25 × 2.25\times measured speedup ( 0.464 0.464 s vs. 1.044 1.044 s) over the DDIM-50 teacher. At comparable latency, TamedFlow improves FID over the evaluated training-free adaptive baselines (e.g., FoCa at FID 2.65 2.65 , 0.466 0.466 s). Controlled ablations support trajectory supervision and learned routing at nearly matched latency, while evaluations on ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 , MS-COCO, and Latte video DiTs extend the empirical scope. In summary, our contributions are: • Diagnostic and analysis of the Combination Gap. We document the failure of applying the evaluated adaptive reuse methods to a compressed DiT, and derive a DDIM rollout bound characterizing how sequential drafting can amplify local velocity errors. • Trajectory-stabilized speculative distillation. We introduce TamedFlow, uniting feature alignment, residual velocity correction, and randomized rollout supervision to optimize a compressed DiT for autonomous multi-step drafting. • Learned routing and deployment evaluation. We propose an asymmetric execution policy via a 4M-parameter LTE to accept reliable drafts or trigger teacher rescue, evaluating quality–latency trade-offs across resolutions, text conditioning, and video alongside physical deployment costs. 2 Related Work Prior work on DiT acceleration reduces the number of solver evaluations, the cost of each evaluation, or the teacher computation retained during adaptive execution. TamedFlow studies their interface: whether a compressed student can reliably replace short segments of a teacher trajectory. 2.1 Step Count Reduction in Diffusion and Flow Models Step reduction lowers the number of solver evaluations. Higher-order solvers improve numerical efficiency for a fixed model ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , while distillation changes the model: progressive distillation shortens the schedule ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , consistency models match predictions across noise levels ( Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) , MeanFlow and Model-Guidance alter the target or absorb guidance ( Geng et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . Other formulations align distributions or scores, distill autoregressively, transfer trajectories, or train few-step students adversarially ( Yin et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) . These methods optimize a sparse standalone sampler deployed entirely on its own. TamedFlow instead retains a multi-step teacher as a reliable safeguard and uses the student to propose short trajectory segments whose acceptance is decided adaptively online. A related line studies trajectory geometry. Rectified flow and InstaFlow construct straighter paths ( Liu et al., 2023 ) ; interpolant transformers unify diffusion and flow parametrizations ( Ma et al., 2024a ) ; and guided path sampling corrects trajectories during integration ( Li et al., 2026 ) . TCD and Hyper-SD learn consistency or trajectory segments for few-step sampling ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2024 ) . TamedFlow keeps the teacher path as the reference, trains a cross-architecture student for selectively accepted rollouts, and retains teacher rescue in the deployed sampler. 2.2 Per-Step Compute Acceleration and Feature Caching Per-step methods keep the schedule while avoiding full recomputation. Feature-reuse methods cache activations across timesteps or blocks ( Ma et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2026b ; Wimbauer et al., 2024 ) ; forecasting methods extrapolate future features ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Cai et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) ; and learned schedulers select policies per sample ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . These methods exploit local regularity in intermediate computations. Our same-student diagnostic shows that their evaluated configurations do not transfer directly to the compressed student, but does not isolate a universal caching failure mechanism. Most reuse methods leave the model unchanged and decide which internal computations can be skipped. TamedFlow instead trains the student under rollout supervision and learns whether an entire student-generated segment can advance without a teacher call. DisCa ( Zou et al., 2026a ) also studies incompatibility between step-distilled video DiTs and feature caches, but repairs the cache side with a predictor and Restricted MeanFlow schedule. TamedFlow acts on the draft student instead. 2.3 Speculative Verification in Generative Paradigms Speculative decoding verifies proposed tokens with a target model ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ) ; causal masking permits parallel verification and exact correction. Diffusion lacks this structure because each teacher state depends on the preceding prediction. Replaying a K K -step draft exactly would require sequential teacher evaluations and remove much of the saving. SpecDiff ( Pan et al., 2026 ) studies self-speculative diffusion under this constraint. TamedFlow replaces exact verification with learned trajectory estimation. The LTE scores student-internal features after a draft using rollout agreement as its training target. Accepted drafts avoid the teacher; rejected drafts return to the pre-draft state for one teacher step. Routing is therefore inexpensive and online, but approximate and not distribution-preserving by construction. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries: Diffusion Models, DiT, and Flow Matching Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) learn to reverse a gradual noising process, so generation requires a sequence of state-dependent model evaluations. Teacher offloading and weight quantization represent orthogonal opportunities to mitigate co-residency overhead in production. 5 Conclusion In this work, we introduced TamedFlow, an acceleration framework that reconciles parameter compression with adaptive execution for Diffusion Transformers. By training a compact student for short-horizon trajectory agreement and employing asymmetric routing with selective teacher rescue, TamedFlow achieves FID 2.58 2.58 at 2.25 × 2.25\times speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , with transfer evaluated across resolutions, text conditioning, and video. Our findings show that pointwise alignment can leave compounding trajectory divergence during autonomous drafting, creating the Combination Gap. Controlled ablations support rollout supervision, and routing controls favor LTE over random decisions at nearly matched latency, suggesting that compression and adaptive inference can be made compatible when the compact model is trained as a multi-step drafter and the sampler retains a recovery path back to the teacher.
